lead: Today Paul cries out, “See, now is the acceptable time”, and describes an apostle's life as a string of paradoxes: sorrowful yet always rejoicing, having nothing yet possessing everything. In the Gospel Jesus says, “I am the light of the world.” The light of Christ shines most clearly in lives like Paul's, where human weakness and God's power meet. The key words are now and light.

set: Paul has just written that God “reconciled us to himself through Christ” and made him an ambassador with the message “be reconciled to God” (5:18–20). Now he urges the Corinthians not to let that grace go to waste, and he quotes Isaiah 49:8 in its Greek form. He then defends his ministry, not by listing successes, but by listing what he has suffered and how God has carried him through.
str: vv. 1–2: do not accept God's grace in vain; now is the day of salvation.
vv. 3–7: the servants of God commend themselves by endurance and by the gifts of the Spirit.
vv. 8–10: seven paradoxes of the apostolic life.
kw: Isaiah's Greek text had dektos, “acceptable”. Paul repeats the word with a stronger form, “most acceptable”. The time of God's favour that the prophet promised has arrived.
Paul says it twice: “now is the acceptable time; now is the day of salvation”. The grace of God is never only for later. It meets us today.
vv: As we work together with him, we urge you also not to accept the grace of God in vain.
Paul calls himself a co-worker with God. Grace is pure gift, but it can be received “in vain” if it does not change the life of the one who receives it.
See, now is the acceptable time; see, now is the day of salvation!
Paul adds his own comment to the prophet's words. He does not wait for a better moment to call his readers to conversion.
as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing everything.
These lines describe Christ himself, who “though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor” (8:9). The apostle shares the pattern of his Lord.
ch: The Catechism quotes 2 Corinthians 6:2 when it speaks of the Last Judgement: the message of the Judgement calls people to conversion while God is still giving them “the acceptable time” and “the day of salvation” (CCC 1041). The Church has always seen in Paul's list of paradoxes a portrait of every faithful pastor and every Christian who suffers for Christ. What looks like loss is gain, because the life of Jesus is made visible in mortal flesh (4:10–11).

r.h: I am the light of the world
set: John sets these words at the festival of Booths (7:2). During that feast great lamps were lit in the Court of the Women in the Temple, and the light was said to shine over all Jerusalem. Jesus speaks “in the treasury of the temple” (8:20), which was in that same court. In the oldest manuscripts today's passage (8:12) follows directly on 7:52; the story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11) is missing there and was placed here later, though the Church receives it as inspired Scripture.
The Pharisees object that a man cannot be a witness in his own case. Jesus answers that he is not alone: the Father bears witness with him.
str: v. 12: “I am the light of the world.”
vv. 13–18: the debate about valid testimony: Jesus and the Father as two witnesses.
vv. 19–20: “Where is your Father?”; his hour has not yet come.
kw: egō eimi to phōs tou kosmou
I am the light of the world

One of the great “I am” sayings in John. In the Old Testament light belongs to God: “The Lord is my light and my salvation” (Psalm 27:1). The Law too was called a lamp (Psalm 119:105). Jesus claims to be what the feast's lamps only pointed to.
A key word of John's Gospel. The Law required two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jesus' second witness is the Father, who speaks through his works and through the Scriptures (5:36–39).
vv: I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will never walk in darkness but will have the light of life.
The promise is for those who “follow”, a word for discipleship. The pillar of fire led Israel through the desert at night (Exodus 13:21). Now the light walks ahead of us in person.
You judge by human standards; I judge no one.
Literally, “according to the flesh”, that is, by appearances. Jesus came not to condemn but to save (3:17).
You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would know my Father also.
To know Jesus is to know the Father. Later Jesus says to Philip, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (14:9).
ch: The Church confesses Christ as “Light from Light” in the Creed. The Fathers called Baptism “enlightenment”, because those who receive it are filled with the light of the Word (CCC 1216). The Second Vatican Council begins its document on the Church with the words Lumen Gentium, “Christ is the light of the nations”, and adds that this light shines on the face of the Church (Lumen Gentium 1). The Church has no light of her own; she reflects his.

qa: Is Jesus attacking the Pharisees in this passage?

John shows a sharp debate, but Jesus is not rejecting the Pharisees as people. Many of them shared his faith in the resurrection and his love for the Law, and Nicodemus, a Pharisee, became a disciple (3:1; 19:39). The question at stake is who Jesus is, and it is put to every reader.
study: Paul says “now is the acceptable time”. What step toward God have I been putting off for later?
Where in my home or work do I most need the light of Christ to drive out darkness?
